# Likelihood {#sec-likelihood}

{{< include ../../_figures/part2/likelihood-shared.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-note .learning-objectives .reader-only title="Learning objectives" appearance="simple"}

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

1. construct a likelihood from an independent sampling model and its parameter space;
2. distinguish a likelihood from a probability distribution and compute an MLE;
3. interpret score, expected Fisher information, and observed information;
4. use the Cramér–Rao bound and the large-sample Normal approximation with their stated conditions.

The **core route** runs through likelihood, log-likelihood, MLE, information, and the approximate distribution of the MLE. Sufficiency and the long proofs marked *not examinable* are optional enrichment.
:::

The **likelihood** is obtained by evaluating the **joint density (or probability mass function)** at the observed data:

$$
f(\underline{x} \mid \theta),
\quad \underline{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n).
$$

It plays a central role in both **frequentist** and **Bayesian** statistics.

The same mathematical expression has two different roles. As a function of the data it is a probability model; as a function of $\theta$ with the observed data fixed it is a likelihood. A likelihood gives **relative support** for parameter values—it is not generally a probability distribution over $\theta$, need not integrate to $1$ over $\theta$, and a density value is not itself a probability.

::: {#imp-notation-freq-vs-bayes .callout-important collapse="true" appearance="simple"}

### Notation Convention

* When **specifying the distribution of the data** in the frequentist setting, we write

  $$
  X_i \sim \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
  $$

  to emphasise that $\theta$ is fixed (but unknown).

* When writing **densities**, we will always use

  $$
  f(\underline{x}\mid\theta).
  $$

  * In the **frequentist** context: read this as *“the ***joint density*** of the data when the parameter takes the value $\theta$.”*
  * In the **Bayesian** context: it is literally the **conditional density** of the data given the **random** parameter $\theta$.
  
* Later, in the **Bayesian** parts of the course, we will also use

  $$
  X_i \mid \theta \sim \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
  $$

  where the bar $\mid \theta$ reflects its probabilistic meaning: *conditioning on random parameters*.
:::


## Likelihoods Under Independence and Dependence {#sec-likelihood-dependence}

The form of the likelihood depends crucially on whether our observations are independent and identically distributed ([i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"}), merely independent, or dependent. These three cases look similar but lead to different joint densities. 

::: {.panel-tabset}
### [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"} data

**This is the default case in most of this course.**

Suppose $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are **independent and identically distributed ([i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"})** random variables:

$$
X_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
\quad i = 1, \ldots, n.
$$

Each $X_i$ has density (or PMF)

$$
f(x \mid \theta).
$$

Then the **joint density** of the full sample is

$$
f(x_1, \ldots, x_n \mid \theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid \theta).
$$

### Independent (not identical) data


If instead the samples are **independent but not identically distributed**:

$$
X_i \sim \mathrm{Distribution}_i(\theta),
$$

with individual densities $f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta)$, then the joint density becomes

$$
f(x_1, \ldots, x_n \mid \theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^n f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta).
$$


### Dependent data

In many real-world situations, data are **dependent**.

**Example:** Suppose our data are daily temperatures in Newcastle upon Tyne. Yesterday's temperature will influence today's temperature, and today's temperature will influence tomorrow's.

In such cases, we must model the dependencies explicitly. For instance,

$$
X_{t+1} \mid X_t = x_t  \sim \mathcal{N}(x_t, \sigma^2).
$$

The likelihood is still the **joint distribution**, but expressed as an initial density followed by a product of **conditional densities**:

$$
f(x_1,\ldots,x_n \mid \sigma^2) 
= f(x_1\mid\sigma^2)\prod_{t=2}^n f(x_t \mid x_{t-1}, \sigma^2).
$$

The initial model $f(x_1\mid\sigma^2)$ must be specified; otherwise the joint model is incomplete.

The example above assumed a Markov property (each observation only depends on the previous one). In general, observations may depend on the entire history, in which case the joint density factorises via the <span class="xref-no-num">[chain rule @prp-chain-rule]</span>:
$$
f(x_1,\ldots,x_n \mid \theta) = f(x_1\mid\theta)\prod_{t=2}^n f(x_t \mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1},\theta)
$$


::: {.callout-warning #wrn-nonexaminable-dependent-likelihood}
#### Non-Examinable Content
This course focuses only on the **i.i.d.** or **independent** case.  

Dependent data will be covered in later modules and is **not examinable**.
:::

:::


| Case                          | Assumption                                                | Factorisation of Joint Density |
|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **[i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"} data**               | Independent and identically distributed; each with density $f(x\mid\theta)$ | $f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i\mid\theta)$ |
| **Independent (not identical) data** | Independent; each $X_i$ may have its own density $f_{X_i}(x_i\mid\theta)$ | $f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_{X_i}(x_i\mid\theta)$ |
| **Dependent data (general)**  | Dependent; factorise using the <span class="xref-no-num">[chain rule @prp-chain-rule]</span>                 | $f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = f(x_1\mid\theta)\prod_{t=2}^n f(x_t \mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1},\theta)$ |


::: {.callout-warning}
#### Reminder: Non-Examinable Content

The **dependent case** in the above table is shown for completeness.

This course focuses only on the **i.i.d.** or **independent** case, and the dependent case is **not examinable**.
:::

::: {.remark #rem-products}

### Why products?

* Independence means joint probabilities factorise:
  $$
  \mathrm{Pr}(A \cap B) = \mathrm{Pr}(A) \mathrm{Pr}(B).
  $$
* By the same <span class="xref-no-num">[rule @def-independence-rv]</span>, the joint density of independent random variables is the product of their individual densities.
* This is a common **misconception**: without independence, you **cannot** just multiply.

:::

## Likelihood Function

So far we have described the likelihood informally as “the joint density of the data given the parameter.”

We now give a **formal definition** of the *likelihood function* and introduce the notation we will use in the **frequentist parts** of the course.

::: {.definition #def-likelihood}
### Likelihood Function

For fixed observed data $\underline{x}$, the **likelihood function** is defined as

$$
L(\theta ; \underline{x}) \coloneqq f(\,\underline{x} \mid \theta).
$$

Here we treat $\theta$ as the **variable**, and the data $\underline{x}$ as fixed.
The domain is the parameter space $\Theta$ (for example, $p\in[0,1]$, $\lambda\geq0$, or $\sigma^2>0$).
:::


### Illustration (Likelihood with a coin)

Suppose we toss a possibly biased coin twice, where

$$
\Pr(\text{Head})=\theta, 
\qquad 
\Pr(\text{Tail})=1-\theta.
$$

Let $X$ be the number of heads in two tosses. Then, since this is a <span class="xref-no-num">[Binomial @sec-binom]</span> observation:

$$
f(x\mid\theta)=\Pr(X=x\mid\theta)
=\binom{2}{x}\theta^x(1-\theta)^{2-x},
\qquad x=0,1,2.
$$

There are *two* interpretations of this:

1. **Probability view (before observing data).**  
  For fixed $\theta$, this is a *probability mass function* (PMF) in $x$.  It satisfies
  $$
  f(x=0 \mid \theta) + f(x=1 \mid \theta) + f(x = 2 \mid \theta) = 1.
  $$
  It tells us how likely different data values $x$ are under parameter $\theta$.

2. **Likelihood view (after observing data).**  
  Now suppose we observe $x=2$. Now, since $x=2$ is fixed, the same formula becomes
  $$
  L(\theta; x=2) = f(2\mid\theta) = \theta^2.
  $$
  This function tells us how plausible different values of $\theta$ are, given the observed data.

---

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Show Visualisation</strong></summary>
```

{{< include ../../_figures/part2/binomial-likelihood.qmd >}}

```{=html}
</details>
```

---

**Interpretation**

Consider two **competing** values of $\theta$ for observing $x=2$ heads in $n=2$ tosses:  

1. If **$\theta=0.01$**, the probability of observing $X=2$ is
  $$
  L(0.01;2)=0.0001.
  $$
  For such a coin, two heads would be highly unusual.

1. If **$\theta=0.99$**, the probability of observing $X=2$ is
  $$
  L(0.99;2)=0.9801 \approx 0.98.
  $$
  For such a coin, observing $X=2$ is exactly what we’d expect.

Given $x=2$, values of $\theta$ close to $1$ are much more plausible than values near $0$.

::: {.remark #rem-lik-vs-prob}
### Likelihood vs. Probability

It is important to distinguish between the **joint density** of the data and the **likelihood function**:

* **Joint density (PDF/PMF).**
  $f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)$ is viewed as a function of the *data* $\underline{x}$, with the parameter $\theta$ fixed.
  This describes the probability distribution of the sample under $\theta$.

* **Likelihood function.**
  The same expression, written as

  $$
  L(\theta;\underline{x}) = f(\underline{x}\mid\theta),
  $$

  is instead viewed as a function of the *parameter* $\theta$, with the observed data $\underline{x}$ held fixed.
  This is the function we use to make inferences about $\theta$.

  It is **not** a posterior distribution: areas under a likelihood curve are not probabilities for $\theta$ unless a Bayesian prior is supplied and the result is normalised.

---

In short:

* **Joint density**: given $\theta$, how *likely* are different data values $\underline{x}$?
* **Likelihood**: given observed $\underline{x}$, how *plausible* are different values of $\theta$?

:::

::: {.callout-tip .checkpoint .reader-only title="Checkpoint: what is varying?" appearance="simple"}
In $f(2\mid\theta)=\theta^2$, ask which quantity is held fixed. If $\theta$ is fixed and $x$ varies, this belongs to a PMF. If $x=2$ is fixed and $\theta$ varies over $[0,1]$, it is a likelihood. Explain why the second curve is not required to sum or integrate to $1$ over $\theta$.
:::



### Computing Likelihood Functions {#sec-computing-likelihoods}

This is a **very important skill** in the course: you will use it often in the *frequentist* parts, and it is **essential** for the *Bayesian* part.

---

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Guide to Computing Likelihood Functions</strong></summary>
```

The general strategy is:

1. **Check the model carefully.** Look for:

   * Are the data **[i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"}** or just **independent**?
   * How many **data points** are observed?
   * What notation is used for the data ($X_i$, $Y_i$, $Z_i$, …)?
   * What notation is used for the parameters ($\mu$, $\alpha$, $\gamma$, $\theta$, …)?
   * What is the **parameter space**, and what restrictions define the support of the data?

   *(In the examples below we assume $n$ independent data points $X_1,\dots,X_n$ with parameter $\theta$. If there is only one data point, the likelihood is just its PDF/PMF.)*

2. **Write down the PDF/PMF of one observation.**

   $$
   f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta)
   $$

3. **Multiply to form the joint density**, i.e. the likelihood:

   $$
   L(\theta ; \underline{x}) 
   = f(\underline{x} \mid \theta) 
   = \prod_{i=1}^n f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta).
   $$


#### Common Mistakes {.unnumbered}

It is **very easy** to slip up when multiplying terms. Watch out for:

1. **Forgetting the index.**
   Always use $x_i$ inside the product.

   Example (Exponential model):
   If $X_i \sim \mathrm{Exponential}(\theta)$ with density

   $$
   f(x_i \mid \theta) = \theta e^{-\theta x_i}, \quad x_i > 0,
   $$

   then the likelihood is

   $$
   f(\underline{x} \mid \theta) 
   = \prod_{i=1}^n \theta e^{-\theta x_i} 
   = \theta^n \exp\!\left(-\theta \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right).
   $$

   A common mistake is to write

   $$
   \prod_{i=1}^n \theta e^{-\theta x} = \theta^n e^{-\theta n x} \quad \text{(wrong!)}
   $$

   which ignores the index on $x_i$.

2. **Oversimplifying.**
   Many likelihoods look messy — that is normal!

   Example (Gamma model):
   If $X_i \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha, \theta)$ with density

   $$
   f(x_i \mid \alpha, \theta) 
   = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha}\, x_i^{\alpha - 1} e^{-x_i/\theta}, 
   \quad x_i > 0,
   $$

   then the likelihood is

   $$
   f(\underline{x} \mid \alpha, \theta) 
   = \left(\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha}\right)^n 
     \left(\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha - 1}\right)
     \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right).
   $$

   Notice how the product

   $$
   \prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha - 1}
   $$

   cannot be simplified further (unless you introduce the geometric mean[^geometric-mean]).

#### A Safe Strategy {.unnumbered}

When starting out, it is helpful to **expand the product term by term**:

$$
f(\underline{x} \mid \theta) 
= f(x_1 \mid \theta) 
\times f(x_2 \mid \theta) 
\times \cdots 
\times f(x_n \mid \theta).
$$

Then simplify step by step.

This is slower, but it reduces errors. With practice, you’ll be able to simplify likelihoods much more quickly.

```{=html}
</details>
```

:::

---

::: {.example #exm-bern-likelihood}
### Bernoulli Likelihood
Suppose we have $n$ [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"} data distributed according to the <span class="xref-no-num">[Bernoulli distribution @sec-bern]</span>:

$$
  Y_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).
$$
Derive the **likelihood function**.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

Because the $Y_i$ are [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"}, the joint PMF factorises:

$$
L(p;\underline{y}) = f(\underline{y}\mid p) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i \mid p).
$$

For the Bernoulli distribution,

$$
f(y_i \mid p) = p^{y_i}(1-p)^{1-y_i}.
$$

Hence,

\begin{align*}
L(p; \underline{y}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p^{y_i}(1 - p)^{1-y_i} \\ 
&= p^{y_1} (1-p)^{1-y_1} \times p^{y_2} (1-p)^{1-y_2} \times \ldots \times p^{y_n} (1-p)^{1-y_n} \\ 
&= p^{y_1 + \ldots + y_n} (1 - p)^{(1-y_1) + \ldots + (1-y_n)} \\ 
&= p^{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i} (1-p)^{\sum_{i=1}^n 1 - y_i}.
\end{align*}

Writing $\sum_{i=1}^n y_i = n\bar{y}$ gives

$$
L(p;\underline{y}) = p^{n\bar{y}}(1-p)^{n(1-\bar{y})}.
$$


```{=html}
</details>
```

:::


In practice, and in **assessed questions** in this course, it is important to be comfortable with computing likelihood functions for actual observed data. The next example does this:

::: {#exm-bern-likelihood-data}
### Bernoulli Likelihood with Data
Suppose $n=5$ [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"} observations $X_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ are observed as
$$
\underline{x} = (1,0,1,1,0).
$$
Derive the **likelihood function** and evaluate it for a few values of $p$.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

Since $\underline{x}  = (1,0,1,1,0)$, we have $\sum_i x_i = 3$. Therefore:
$$
L(p ; \underline{x}) = p^3 (1-p)^2.
$$

  * If $p=0.5$, $L(0.5) = 0.5^3 \cdot 0.5^2 = 0.03125$.
  * If $p=0.7$, $L(0.7) = 0.7^3 \cdot 0.3^2 \approx 0.0309$.
  * If $p=0.8$, $L(0.8) = 0.8^3 \cdot 0.2^2 = 0.0205$.

So the data are slightly more likely under $p=0.5$ than $p=0.8$.


```{=html}
</details>
```


:::

::: {.remark #rem-bernoulli-binomial-likelihood}
### Bernoulli sequence versus Binomial count

For the exact sequence $(1,0,1,1,0)$, the Bernoulli likelihood is $p^3(1-p)^2$. If we retain only the count $X=3$ out of $5$, the Binomial likelihood is $\binom53p^3(1-p)^2$. The expressions differ by $\binom53$, which does not depend on $p$, so they have the same shape as functions of $p$ and the same MLE. This is an early example of data reduction: for this model, the number of successes contains the information about $p$ needed for likelihood-based inference.
:::

::: {#exm-normal-likelihood}
### Normal Likelihood

Suppose we have $n$ [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"} data distributed according to the <span class="xref-no-num">[Normal distribution @sec-normal]</span>:

$$
  T_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \gamma).
$$

Derive the **likelihood function**.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

Because the $T_i$ are [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"}, the joint PDF factorises:

$$
L(\mu, \gamma ;\underline{t}) = f(\underline{t}\mid \mu, \gamma) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(t_i \mid \mu, \gamma).
$$

For the Normal distribution (with variance $\gamma = \sigma^2$),

$$
f(t_i \mid \mu, \gamma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \gamma}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{1}{2\gamma} (t_i - \mu)^2 \right\}.
$$

Hence,

\begin{align*}
L(\mu, \gamma ;\underline{t}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \gamma}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{1}{2\gamma} (t_i - \mu)^2 \right\} \\
&= (2\pi \gamma)^{-\tfrac{n}{2}} \exp\left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n -\frac{1}{2\gamma} (t_i - \mu)^2 \right\}.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

$$
L(\mu, \gamma ;\underline{t}) = (2\pi \gamma)^{-\tfrac{n}{2}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{1}{2\gamma} \sum_{i=1}^n  (t_i - \mu)^2 \right\}.
$$




```{=html}
</details>
```


:::


::: {#exm-poisson-likelihood}
### Poisson Likelihood

Suppose we have $n$ [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"} data distributed according to the <span class="xref-no-num">[Poisson distribution @sec-pois]</span>:

$$
  V_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\alpha)
$$

Derive the **likelihood function**.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

Because the $V_i$ are [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"}, the joint PMF factorises:

$$
L(\alpha ;\underline{v}) = f(\underline{v}\mid \alpha) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(v_i \mid \alpha).
$$

For the Poisson distribution

$$
f(v_i \mid \alpha) = \frac{\alpha^{v_i} e^{-\alpha}}{v_i!}
$$

Hence,

\begin{align*}
L(\alpha ;\underline{v}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n  \frac{\alpha^{v_i} e^{-\alpha}}{v_i!} \\
&= \alpha^{n\bar{v}} e^{-n\alpha} \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{v_i!}
\end{align*}

Therefore,

$$
L(\alpha ;\underline{v}) = \alpha^{n\bar{v}} e^{-n\alpha} \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{v_i!}.
$$


```{=html}
</details>
```

:::

### Data Reduction and Sufficient Statistics (not examinable) {#sec-sufficiency}

When we write down a likelihood, the parameter often only depended on the sample through a few summaries (e.g. a sum or a mean). 

**Sufficiency** formalises when such a summary contains *all the information in the sample about* the parameter $\theta$.

::: {.definition #def-sufficient}
#### Sufficient Statistic
Let $\underline{X}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ have joint PDF/PMF $f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)$.  

A statistic $T(\underline{X})$ is **sufficient** for $\theta$ if the conditional distribution of the data given the statistic does **not** depend on $\theta$, i.e.
$$
f(\underline{x}\mid T(\underline{x})=t,\ \theta)\ \text{does not depend on } \theta.
$$
:::

::: {.theorem #thm-factorisation}
#### Neyman–Fisher Factorisation
$T(\underline{X})$ is sufficient for $\theta$ **if and only if** there exist functions $g(\theta, T(\underline{x}))$ and $h(\underline{x})$ such that
$$
f_{\underline{X}}(\underline{x}\mid \theta)=g \big(\theta, T(\underline{x})\big)\,h(\underline{x}).
$$
:::

::: {#exm-sufficient-bin-bern}
### Sufficiency: Bernoulli model
If $X_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(p)$ i.i.d. and $y=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$, then
$$
L(p;\underline{x})=f_{\underline{X}}(\underline{x}\mid p)
=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}
=p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{n-\sum x_i}
=\underbrace{p^{y}(1-p)^{n-y}}_{g(p,\,y)}\ \underbrace{1}_{h(\underline{x})}.
$$
By factorisation, $T(\underline{X})=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ is sufficient for $p$.
:::

::: {#exm-sufficient-pois}
### Sufficiency: Poisson model
If $X_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ i.i.d. and $y=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$, then
$$
L(\lambda;\underline{x})=f_{\underline{X}}(\underline{x}\mid \lambda)
=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x_i}}{x_i!}
=\underbrace{e^{-n\lambda}\lambda^{\sum x_i}}_{g(\lambda,\,y)}
\ \underbrace{\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{x_i!}}_{h(\underline{x})},
$$
so $T(\underline{X})=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ is sufficient for $\lambda$.
:::

::: {#exm-sufficient-norm}
### Sufficiency: Normal model
If $X_i \sim \mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ i.i.d.:

- **Known $\sigma^2$.** With $\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum x_i$,
$$
f_{\underline{X}}(\underline{x}\mid \mu)
=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right]
=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\,
\underbrace{\exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})^2\right]}_{h(\underline{x})}\,
\underbrace{\exp\!\left[-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\bar{x}-\mu)^2\right]}_{g(\mu,\,\bar{x})}.
$$
Hence $T(\underline{X})=\bar{X}$ is sufficient for $\mu$.

- **Unknown $\sigma^2$.** Write $S^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar{X})^2$. Then
$$
f_{\underline{X}}(\underline{x}\mid \mu,\sigma^2)
=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\Big\{\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})^2}_{(n-1)s^2}
+n(\bar{x}-\mu)^2\Big\}\right]
=\underbrace{(2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(0)}_{h(\underline{x})}\,
\underbrace{(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(n-1)s^2+n(\bar{x}-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]}_{g\big((\mu,\sigma^2),\,(\bar{x},s^2)\big)}.
$$
Thus $T(\underline{X})=(\bar{X},S^2)$ is jointly sufficient for $(\mu,\sigma^2)$.
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
### Common misconceptions
- Sufficiency is **model-dependent**: change the sampling model, and what’s sufficient may change.  
- *Sufficient* ≠ *efficient*: it tells us what data features matter for $\theta$, not how variable an estimator is.  
- Although not explicitly mentioned, we will **reuse** these $T$ when we derive MLEs and, later in the Bayesian chapter, when posteriors update via the same statistics.
:::

## Maximum Likelihood Estimation

::: {.definition #def-mle}
### Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE)

For observed data $\underline x$, a **maximum likelihood estimate** is a parameter value that maximises the likelihood over the full parameter space:

$$
\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \argmax_{\theta \in \Theta} \, L(\theta ; \underline{x}).
$$

Before the data are observed, replacing $\underline x$ by the random sample $\underline X$ defines the **maximum likelihood estimator** $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}(\underline X)$.

Solving a score equation finds only interior stationary-point **candidates**. To identify the MLE, check the parameter space, compare all candidates, verify maxima rather than minima, and inspect any boundaries. The maximiser can also be non-unique.
:::

::: {#imp-term-argmax-max .callout-important collapse="false" appearance="simple"}

### Terminology: $\argmax$ vs. $\max$

The $\max$ gives the **largest value** attained by a function.
$$
\max_{\theta \in \Theta} L(\theta ; \underline{X})
$$
means “the maximum likelihood value.”

The $\argmax$ gives the **argument (input)** where the maximum occurs.
$$
\argmax_{\theta \in \Theta} L(\theta ; \underline{X})
$$
means “the parameter value that maximises the likelihood.”

So: $\max$ is the **height**, $\argmax$ is the **location**.

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Show Visualisation </strong></summary>
```

{{< include ../../_figures/part2/argmax-versus-max.qmd >}}

```{=html}
</details>
```

:::

:::

Because the logarithm is a **monotonically increasing function**, the value of $\theta$ that maximises the likelihood will also maximise the **log-likelihood**.  

In practice, we almost always work with the log-likelihood because it is **simpler to handle mathematically**: it turns products into sums, and derivatives are easier to compute.  


::: {.definition #def-log-likelihood}
### Log-Likelihood

The **log-likelihood** is defined as

$$
\ell(\theta ; \underline{x}) = \log L(\theta ; \underline{x}).
$$

- This is literally just the logarithm of the likelihood.  
- Because $\log$ is increasing, maximising $\ell(\theta;\underline{x})$ gives the same $\hat{\theta}$ as maximising $L(\theta;\underline{x})$.  

:::


---


Keyboard users can focus the likelihood surface and use the arrow keys. The text readout beneath the plots reports the selected values and log-likelihood.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
## ✨ Big picture:
* The <span class="xref-no-num">[likelihood function @def-likelihood]</span>  tells us how **plausible** each parameter value is, given the data.
* The <span class="xref-no-num">[MLE @def-mle]</span> chooses the parameter value that makes the observed data most likely.
* Later, in Bayesian inference, we will combine the likelihood with a **prior distribution** on $\theta$ to obtain a **posterior distribution**.
:::

### Computing Univariate MLEs {#sec-computing-univariate-mles}

::: {.example #exm-bern-mle}
### Bernoulli MLE

From @exm-bern-likelihood, we saw that the likelihood function for $n$ i.i.d. $Y_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ observations was

$$ 
 L(p;\underline{y}) = p^{n\bar{y}}(1-p)^{n(1-\bar{y})}.
$$

Compute the MLE of $p$.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

From the provided likelihood, we first compute the **log-likelihood**:

$$
\ell(p ; \underline{y})
= \Big(\sum_i y_i \Big)\log p + \Big(n-\sum_i y_i\Big)\log(1-p).
$$
Differentiate and solve:
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial p}\ell(p ; \underline{y})
= \frac{\sum_i y_i}{p} - \frac{n - \sum_i y_i}{1-p} = 0.
$$
This gives
$$
\hat{p}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i,
$$

the **sample proportion of successes**.


```{=html}
</details>
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip #tip-bernoulli-estimator-mle appearance="simple"}
### Recurring Bernoulli example: the same rule, a new justification

In @exm-bernoulli-estimator, $\bar Y$ was introduced because it is unbiased with variance $p(1-p)/n$. The likelihood argument now gives
$$
\hat p_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\bar Y.
$$
Thus one formula can be justified in two ways: by its repeated-sampling properties and by maximising the support the observed data give to $p$. In Chapter 6 a Beta prior will produce a posterior mean and MAP estimate that modify this rule using prior counts.
:::

::: {.example #exm-binom-mle-single}
### Binomial MLE
Suppose we have a **single** <span class="xref-no-num">[Binomial @sec-binom]</span> observation
$$
X \sim \textrm{Bin}(n, \theta).
$$
Derive the **maximum likelihood estimator** of $\theta$.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

Since we only have **one** observation, the likelihood function is just the distribution of the observation:

$$
L(\theta ; x) = f(x \mid \theta) = \binom{n}{x} \theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}.
$$

The log-likelihood is thus

$$
\ell(\theta; x) = \log f(x \mid \theta) = \log\left(\binom{n}{x}\right) + x\log\theta + (n-x)\log(1-\theta).
$$

Differentiating, we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\,\ell(\theta;x)
= \frac{x}{\theta} - \frac{n-x}{1-\theta}.
$$

Setting the derivative to zero and solving,

$$
\frac{x}{\theta} = \frac{n-x}{1-\theta}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
x(1-\theta) = (n-x)\theta
\;\Longrightarrow\;
x = n\theta
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\hat\theta = \frac{x}{n}.
$$

To confirm it is a maximum, the second derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\,\ell(\theta;x)
= -\frac{x}{\theta^2} - \frac{n-x}{(1-\theta)^2} < 0
\quad \text{for } \theta\in(0,1),
$$

so $\hat\theta=x/n$ maximises the likelihood. (At the boundaries, if $x=0$ then $\hat\theta=0$; if $x=n$ then $\hat\theta=1$.)

```{=html}
</details>
```


:::



::: {.example #exm-binom-mle}
### Another Binomial MLE 
Suppose we have $n$ **independent** Binomial data:
$$
X_i \sim \textrm{Bin}(k_i, \theta).
$$
Note here that each Binomial data has a different number of Bernoulli trials $k_i$, which are known.

Derive the **maximum likelihood estimator** of $\theta$.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

The likelihood function is the joint distribution of the $n$ observations

$$
f(\underline{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \binom{k_i}{x_i} \theta^{x_i}(1-\theta)^{k_i - x_i}.
$$

The log-likelihood is

$$
\ell(\theta;\underline{x}) 
= \sum_{i=1}^n \log\binom{k_i}{x_i}
+ \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\Big)\log\theta
+ \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n (k_i-x_i)\Big)\log(1-\theta).
$$

Let $S=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ (total successes) and $K=\sum_{i=1}^n k_i$ (total trials). Then

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ell(\theta;\underline{x})
= \frac{S}{\theta} - \frac{K-S}{1-\theta}.
$$

Setting to zero and solving:

$$
\frac{S}{\theta} = \frac{K-S}{1-\theta}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
S(1-\theta)=(K-S)\theta
\;\Longrightarrow\;
S=K\theta
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\hat\theta = \frac{S}{K}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n k_i}.
$$

The second derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\ell(\theta;\underline{x})
= -\frac{S}{\theta^2}-\frac{K-S}{(1-\theta)^2}<0
\quad \text{for } \theta\in(0,1),
$$

so this is a (strict) maximum. Boundary cases: if $S=0$ then $\hat\theta=0$; if $S=K$ then $\hat\theta=1$.


```{=html}
</details>
```

:::

::: {.example #exm-pois-mle}
### Poisson MLE

From @exm-poisson-likelihood, we saw that the likelihood function for $n$ i.i.d. $V_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\alpha)$ observations was
$$
L(\alpha ;\underline{v}) = \alpha^{n\bar{v}} e^{-n\alpha} \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{v_i!}.
$$

Derive the **maximum likelihood estimator** of $\alpha$ and determine its **expected value** and **variance**.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

**Step 1: Computing MLE**

The log-likelihood is

$$
\ell(\alpha;\underline{v})
= n\bar v \log \alpha - n\alpha - \sum_{i=1}^n \log(v_i!),
\qquad \alpha \ge 0.
$$

Differentiate w.r.t. $\alpha$:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha}\,\ell(\alpha;\underline{v})
= \frac{n\bar v}{\alpha} - n.
$$

Set to zero and solve:

$$
\frac{n\bar v}{\alpha} - n = 0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\hat\alpha = \bar v = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i.
$$

Second derivative:

$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \alpha^2}\,\ell(\alpha;\underline{v})
= -\frac{n\bar v}{\alpha^2} < 0 \quad (\alpha>0),
$$

so this is a maximum. Boundary case: if all $v_i=0$ (so $\bar v=0$), the likelihood $L(\alpha)=e^{-n\alpha}$ is maximised at $\hat\alpha=0$.

Therefore, the maximum likelihood *estimator* is:

$$
 \hat\alpha = \bar{V}
$$

---

**Step 2: Mean and Variance of $\hat\alpha$**

Recall $\hat\alpha=\bar V=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n V_i$ with $V_i \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Poisson}(\alpha)$.

*Mean*:
$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat\alpha]
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{E}[V_i]
= \frac{1}{n}\cdot n\alpha
= \alpha.
$$

*Variance* (using independence):
$$
\operatorname{Var}[\hat\alpha]
= \operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n V_i\right)
= \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(V_i)
= \frac{1}{n^2}\cdot n\alpha
= \frac{\alpha}{n}.
$$

Here we used $\operatorname{Var}(V_i)=\mathrm{E}[V_i]=\alpha$ for the $\mathrm{Poisson}(\alpha)$ distribution.

```{=html}
</details>
```

:::

::: {.example #exm-normal-mu-mle}
### Normal MLE for $\mu$

From @exm-normal-likelihood, we saw that the likelihood function for $n$ i.i.d. $T_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \gamma)$ observations was
$$ 
  L(\mu, \gamma ;\underline{t}) = (2\pi \gamma)^{-\tfrac{n}{2}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{1}{2\gamma} \sum_{i=1}^n  (t_i - \mu)^2 \right\}.
$$

Suppose that the variance $\gamma$ is *known*. Determine the **MLE** of $\mu$.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

The log-likelihood (as a function of $\mu$) is

$$
\ell(\mu;\underline{t})
= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\gamma) - \frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^n (t_i-\mu)^2.
$$

Differentiating w.r.t. $\mu$,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu}\,\ell(\mu;\underline{t})
= -\frac{1}{2\gamma}\cdot 2\sum_{i=1}^n (t_i-\mu)(-1)
= \frac{1}{\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^n (t_i-\mu).
$$

Setting equal to $0$ and solve:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n (t_i-\mu)=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
n\mu=\sum_{i=1}^n t_i
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\hat\mu=\bar{t}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n t_i.
$$

The second derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\mu^2}\,\ell(\mu;\underline{t})
= -\frac{n}{\gamma}<0,
$$

so $\hat\mu=\bar{t}$ maximises the likelihood.


```{=html}
</details>
```


:::

### Computing Multivariate MLEs

In many practical problems, the statistical model involves more than a single parameter $\theta$. In this case, we work with a **vector of parameters**

$$
\underline{\theta} = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_p).
$$

The definitions of the likelihood function and the MLE extend in a natural way. The main difference is that the optimisation problem now requires solving **simultaneous equations** for each parameter.

::: {#def-multivar-mle}

#### Multivariate MLE

Let $L(\underline{\theta}; \underline{x})$ and $\ell(\underline{\theta}; \underline{x})$ denote the **likelihood** and **log-likelihood** functions respectively, based on observations $\underline{x} = (x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ from a model with parameters $\underline{\theta} = (\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_p)$.

Interior stationary-point candidates can be found by solving the system

$$
\nabla_{\underline{\theta}} \,\ell(\underline{\theta}; \underline{x}) 
\;=\;
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial}{\partial \theta_1}\,\ell(\underline{\theta}; \underline{x}) \\
\dfrac{\partial}{\partial \theta_2}\,\ell(\underline{\theta}; \underline{x}) \\
\vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial}{\partial \theta_p}\,\ell(\underline{\theta}; \underline{x})
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

:::

The score equations are a candidate-generating step, not a complete definition of the MLE. A candidate must be checked using the Hessian or the global shape of the log-likelihood, compared with other candidates, and compared with any parameter-space boundaries. In general this cannot be done in closed form, so in practice we usually rely on *numerical optimisation methods*. We will not cover those methods here; instead, we focus on cases where the global maximiser can be established explicitly.

::: {.example #exm-normal-full-mle}
### Normal MLE for $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$

Suppose we have $n$ i.i.d. observations $X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

Determine the **maximum likelihood estimators** for $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$.

```{=html}
<details>
  <summary><strong> Solution </strong></summary>
```

**Step 1. Compute log-likelihood:** 

The likelihood function is a relabelling of the data terms in @exm-normal-likelihood:

\begin{align*}
L(\mu, \sigma^2 ;\underline{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} (x_i - \mu)^2 \right\} \\
&= (2\pi \sigma^2)^{-\tfrac{n}{2}} \exp\left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} (x_i - \mu)^2 \right\}.
\end{align*}

The log-likelihood is thus

$$
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2;\underline{x}) 
= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) 
- \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2.
$$


**Step 2. Differentiate w.r.t. $\mu$:**

$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mu}
= \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu).
$$

Setting this equal to 0 gives

$$
\hat{\mu} = \bar{x}.
$$

**Step 3. Differentiate w.r.t. $\sigma^2$:**

$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \sigma^2}
= -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2.
$$

Setting this equal to $0$ and substituting $\mu = \hat{\mu}$ gives

$$
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2.
$$

**Final Answer:**
The MLEs are

$$
\hat{\mu} = \bar{X}, 
\qquad
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2.
$$

**Note**: $\hat{\sigma}^2$ is biased (its expectation is $\tfrac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$), but it is the maximum likelihood estimate.


```{=html}
</details>
```


:::

---

## Information and Efficiency of Estimators

In the previous chapter we studied two kinds of *properties of estimators*:

* In <span class="xref-no-num">[Properties of Estimators @sec-estimator-properties]</span>, we introduced: <span class="xref-no-num">[bias @def-bias]</span>, <span class="xref-no-num">[variance @def-variance]</span>, and <span class="xref-no-num">[MSE @def-mse]</span>.  
* In <span class="xref-no-num">[Asymptotic Properties of Estimators @sec-estimator-asymp-properties]</span>, we introduced: <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic unbiasedness @def-asymptotic-unbiasedness]</span> and <span class="xref-no-num">[consistency @def-consistency]</span>.

Now that we have the *likelihood function*, we can go further and introduce two powerful ideas:

* **Cramér–Rao Lower Bound ([CRLB]{title="Cramér–Rao Lower Bound"}):** under regularity conditions, a lower bound on the variance of an unbiased estimator.
* **Efficiency:** whether an estimator actually attains this bound (at least asymptotically).

::: {#imp-crlb-motivation .callout-important collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
### Motivation

Our central measure of estimator quality was the **mean squared error (MSE)**. From the <span class="xref-no-num">[bias-variance decomposition @prp-mse-bias-variance]</span> of the MSE, we know:

$$
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2 + \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}).
$$

For **unbiased estimators** ($\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})=0$), this reduces to

$$
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}).
$$

So if we restrict attention to unbiased estimators, the question of “how good” becomes:

> *Which unbiased estimator has the **smallest possible variance**?*

The Cramér–Rao Lower Bound ([CRLB]{title="Cramér–Rao Lower Bound"}) gives a benchmark for how small the variance can be within this regular, unbiased setting.

:::

Before introducing the [CRLB]{title="Cramér–Rao Lower Bound"} and efficiency, we first need two key definitions derived from the likelihood function.

### Score and Fisher Information

::: {#def-score-statistic}
#### Score Statistic

The **score** is the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter:

$$
U(\theta;\underline{X}) \;=\; \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\,\ell(\theta;\underline{X})
= \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\,\log f(\underline{X}\mid \theta).
$$

It is a **random quantity**.

:::

::: {#def-fisher-information}

#### Fisher Information

The **Fisher information** (or *expected information*) in a sample of size $n$ is the model-average negative curvature of the log-likelihood:

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) \;=\; -\,\mathrm{E}_{\theta}\!\left[ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\,\ell(\theta;\underline{X}) \right].
$$

Under the usual regularity conditions, the equivalent score-variance form is
$$
\mathcal I_n(\theta)=\mathrm E_\theta[U(\theta;\underline X)^2].
$$

:::

**Intuition:** Fisher information measures how much the experiment is expected to tell us about $\theta$ over repeated samples.

* Large expected negative curvature $\Rightarrow$ high expected information.
* Small expected negative curvature $\Rightarrow$ low expected information.

The curvature of the log-likelihood for the **particular observed data** is instead called *observed information*. We define it explicitly near the large-sample approximation below.


::: {#prp-fisher-one-obs}

#### Fisher Information for i.i.d. Data

Suppose we have an i.i.d. sample $\underline{X}^{(n)} = (X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ drawn from the same distribution with PDF/PMF $f(x \mid \theta)$. Define:

* The Fisher information from **one observation**: 
  $$
  \mathcal{I}_1(\theta) = -\mathrm{E}\left [\tfrac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\log f(X\mid \theta)\right]
  $$
* The Fisher information from the **whole sample** (i.e. @def-fisher-information): 
  $$
  \mathcal{I}_n(\theta) = -\mathrm{E}_\theta\left [\tfrac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\ell(\theta;\underline{X}^{(n)})\right]
  $$

Then

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) = n\,\mathcal{I}_1(\theta).
$$

:::

::: {#prf-fisher-one-obs}
For $n$ i.i.d. observations, the log-likelihood is

$$
\ell(\theta;\underline{X}) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(X_i \mid \theta).
$$

Differentiating twice,

$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\ell(\theta;\underline{X}^{(n)}) 
\;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\log f(X_i \mid \theta).
$$

Now take expectations:

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) 
\;=\; -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\ell(\theta;\underline{X}^{(n)}) \right] 
\;=\; -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\log f(X_i \mid \theta)\right].
$$

By linearity of expectation,

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) 
\;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n \left( -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\log f(X_i \mid \theta)\right]\right).
$$

Since the $X_i$ are IID, each term in the sum is the same:

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) = n\,\mathcal{I}_1(\theta).
$$

:::

::: {#imp-compute-fisher-info .callout-important collapse="true" appearance="simple"}

### Computing the Fisher Information of the Whole Sample

In most problems, we work with the **Fisher information for the whole sample**:
$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)
= -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}
   \,\ell(\theta;\underline{X})\right].
$$

For i.i.d. data, there are two standard approaches.

---

**Approach 1: Compute $\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)$ directly**

1. **Write down the likelihood**  
   For $X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Distribution}(\theta)$,
   $$
   L(\theta;\underline{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i\mid\theta).
   $$

2. **Compute the log-likelihood**  
   $$
   \ell(\theta;\underline{x}) = \log L(\theta;\underline{x}).
   $$

3. **Differentiate**  
   Compute the first and second derivatives
   $$
   \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ell(\theta;\underline{x}),
   \qquad
   \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\ell(\theta;\underline{x}).
   $$

4. **Take the expectation**  
   Insert the second derivative into
   $$
   \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)
   = -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[
      \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}
      \ell(\theta;\underline{X})
     \right],
   $$
   where the expectation is taken with respect to the model for $\underline{X}$. You will often use known expressions such as $\mathrm{E}[X_i]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_i)$, obtainable from the *formula sheet*.

---

**Approach 2: Compute $\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)$ and multiply by $n$**

Using @prp-fisher-one-obs, compute the Fisher information for **one observation** and then multiply by $n$.

1. **Write the PDF/PMF for one observation**  
   $$
   f(x\mid\theta).
   $$

2. **Logarithm**  
   $$
   \log f(x\mid\theta).
   $$

3. **Differentiate**  
   $$
   \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f(x\mid\theta),
   \qquad
   \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f(x\mid\theta).
   $$

4. **Compute $\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)$**  
   $$
   \mathcal{I}_1(\theta)
   = -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[
      \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}
      \log f(X\mid\theta)
     \right].
   $$
   Then
   $$
   \mathcal{I}_n(\theta) = n\,\mathcal{I}_1(\theta).
   $$

---

**Recommendation**

- If observations are independent but **not identically distributed**, information is still additive, $\mathcal I(\theta)=\sum_i\mathcal I_i(\theta)$, but the shortcut $n\mathcal I_1(\theta)$ does not apply.
- Even in the i.i.d. case, Approach 1 is often just as quick and avoids memorising extra formulas.  
- For consistency, I therefore recommend **always using Approach 1**.

:::



::: {.example #exm-poisson-fisher}

### Fisher Information for the Poisson Model

Suppose we have $n$ i.i.d. observations $X_i\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\alpha)$. From @exm-poisson-likelihood, we saw the likelihood took the form

$$
L(\alpha; \underline{x}) = \frac{ e^{-\alpha n} \alpha^{n\bar{x}} }{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}
$$

Determine the <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher information @prp-fisher-one-obs]</span> for:

(a) The **whole sample**
(b) A **single observation**


```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Solution</strong></summary>
```

**a. Whole sample**

We have

$$
\ell(\alpha; \underline{x}) = -n\alpha + \bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\bigg)\log \alpha - \sum_{i=1}^n \log x_i!,
\qquad \alpha>0.
$$

Differentiate:

$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \alpha}
= -n + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{\alpha},
\qquad
\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \alpha^2}
= -\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{\alpha^2}.
$$

Hence the Fisher information is

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\alpha)
= -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \alpha^2}\right]
= -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}{\alpha^2}\right]
= \frac{n\alpha}{\alpha^2}
= \frac{n}{\alpha}.
$$

---

**b. Single observation**

For one $X\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\alpha)$,

$$
\ell_1(\alpha;x)=-\alpha + x\log\alpha - \log x!,
\quad
\frac{\partial^2 \ell_1}{\partial \alpha^2}
= -\frac{x}{\alpha^2}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\mathcal{I}_1(\alpha)
= -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ell_1}{\partial \alpha^2}\right]
= -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[-\frac{X}{\alpha^2}\right]
= \frac{\alpha}{\alpha^2}
= \frac{1}{\alpha}.
$$


```{=html}
</details>
```

:::


### Cramér–Rao Lower Bound and Efficiency

We can now state one of the most important results in statistical inference: the **Cramér–Rao inequality**. Under its regularity conditions, it gives a lower benchmark for the variance of an unbiased estimator.

::: {#thm-crlb}
#### The Cramér–Rao Inequality and the [CRLB]{title="Cramér–Rao Lower Bound"}

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be [i.i.d.]{title="Independent and Identically Distributed"} random variables with likelihood function $L(\theta;\underline{x})$, and let $\hat{\theta}$ be an unbiased estimator of $\theta$.

Then, under *regularity conditions*,

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \;\geq\; \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)},
$$
where $\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)$ is the <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher information @prp-fisher-one-obs]</span> for the **whole sample**.

The quantity $\tfrac{1}{\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)}$ is called the **Cramér–Rao Lower Bound ([CRLB]{title="Cramér–Rao Lower Bound"})**. It is a lower benchmark for the variance of regular unbiased estimators; it is **not guaranteed to be attainable**. An estimator is called efficient when it does attain the bound.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" #prf-crlb}
#### Optional proof of the Cramér–Rao inequality (not examinable)

The proof of the Cramér–Rao inequality follows from the **covariance inequality**:

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)^2 \leq \mathrm{Var}(X)\,\mathrm{Var}(Y),
$$

applied to the score random variable $X = U(\theta; \underline{X})$ and the estimator $Y = \hat{\theta}(\underline{X})$. Substituting these in and rearranging for the variance of $\hat{\theta}$ gives

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \;\geq\; \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\theta},U)^2}{\mathrm{Var}(U)}.
$$

Then, under *regularity conditions*, one can show that the variance of $U$ is the Fisher information, and the covariance term equals $1$.

Thus, the proof can be broken into steps:

1. **Prove the Covariance Inequality**
2. **Show:** $\mathrm{E}[U] = 0$
3. **Show:** $\mathrm{Var}(U) = \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)$
4. **Show:** $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\theta}, U) = 1$

Along the way, we will present the regularity conditions.

---

**Step 1 (Proving Covariance Inequality):** 

The covariance inequality follows from the [Cauchy-Schwarz inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Schwarz_inequality) for random variables:

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
#### Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality for Random Variables
For any random variables $X$ and $Y$ of finite variance,
$$
\mathrm{E}[XY]^2 \leq \mathrm{E}[X^2] \mathrm{E}[Y^2].
$$

<details>
<summary><strong>Proof of Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality</strong></summary>

Consider $\mathrm{E}\left[ (aX+Y)^2 \right]$, which is clearly non-negative for real $a$.

Multiplying out gives:
$$
a^2 \mathrm{E}[X^2] + 2a \mathrm{E}[XY] + \mathrm{E}[Y^2] \geq 0.
$$
Consider the left hand side as a quadratic in $a$.
Since it is always non-negative it cannot have two real roots.
Using the quadratic formula the roots satisfy:
$$
a = \frac{-2\mathrm{E}[XY] \pm \sqrt{4 \mathrm{E}[XY]^2 - 4 \mathrm{E}[X^2] \mathrm{E}[Y^2]}}{2 \mathrm{E}[X^2]}
$$
For there to be zero or one real root, the discriminant must be non-positive, i.e.
$$
\mathrm{E}[XY]^2 - \mathrm{E}[X^2] \mathrm{E}[Y^2] \leq 0.
$$
which gives the required result.

</details>


:::


Applying Cauchy-Schwarz, to the mean-zero shifted random variables, $X - \mathrm{E}[X]$ and $Y-\mathrm{E}[Y]$, we obtain

\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)^2 &= \mathrm{E}\left[(X-\mathrm{E}[X])(Y-\mathrm{E}[Y])\right]^2 \\
&\leq \mathrm{E}\left[ (X-\mathrm{E}[X])^2 \right] \mathrm{E}\left[(Y-\mathrm{E}[Y])^2\right]  = \mathrm{Var}(X)\mathrm{Var}(Y).
\end{align*}

---

**Aside:** You may recall that the *correlation* between two random variables is defined as
$$
\mathrm{Cor}(X,Y) = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\mathrm{Var}(X)^{1/2} \mathrm{Var}(Y)^{1/2}}
$$
and satisfies $-1\leq \mathrm{Cor}(X,Y) \leq 1$. This inequality is derived from the **covariance inequality**.

---

**Step 2 (Proving $\mathrm{E}[U] = 0$):**

By the definition of the log-likelihood: 
$$
\tfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta} \ell(\theta;\underline{x}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} \log f(\underline{x} \mid \theta).
$$

Using the chain rule, we have
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} \ell(\theta;\underline{x}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} \log f(\underline{x} \mid \theta) = \frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}.
$$

Since $U(\theta; \underline{x}) = \tfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta} \ell(\theta;\underline{x})$, we can compute its expectation as follows

\begin{align*}
\mathrm{E}[U(\theta; \underline{X})] &= \int U(\theta;\underline{x}) f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} \\
&= \int \frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)} f(\underline{x}\mid\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} \\
&= \int \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} \\
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \int f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} \\
&=  \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} 1 \\
&= 0.
\end{align*}

Here, we assumed the first *regularity condition*:

> **Regularity Condition 1:** We assumed we can interchange the integral and derivative in the step
> $$
> \int \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}  f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \int f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \,\mathrm{d}\underline{x}
> $$


---

**Step 3 (Proving $\mathrm{Var}(U) = \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)$):**

By definition,

$$
\mathrm{Var}(U) = \mathrm{E}[U^2] - \big(\mathrm{E}[U]\big)^2.
$$

From Step 2 we know $\mathrm{E}[U] = 0$, so

$$
\mathrm{Var}(U) = \mathrm{E}[U^2] = \mathrm{E}\!\left[\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\,\ell(\theta;\underline{X})\right)^2\right].
$$

Recall the identity derived in Step 2:
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ell(\theta ; \underline{x})
= \frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) }{f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}.
$$
Differentiating again, using the product and chain rules, yields:

$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ell(\theta ; \underline{x})
= -\frac{ \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \right)^2}{f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)^2} + \frac{\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)} .
$$
Therefore,
$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ell(\theta ; \underline{x})
= -\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ell(\theta;\underline{x})\right)^2 + \frac{\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)} .
$$
Rearranging for $\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ell(\theta;\underline{x})\right)^2$ yields:
$$
\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ell(\theta;\underline{x})\right)^2 = \frac{\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)} - \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ell(\theta ; \underline{x}).
$$

Computing the expectation, we have

\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Var}(U) &= \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} f(\underline{X}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{X}\mid \theta)} - \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ell(\theta ; \underline{X})\right] \\
&= \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} f(\underline{X}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{X}\mid \theta)}\right] + \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[-\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ell(\theta ; \underline{X})\right]}_{= \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)}.
\end{align*}

Concentrating on the remaining expectation:

\begin{align*}
\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} f(\underline{X}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{X}\mid \theta)}\right] &= \int \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \, \mathrm{d}\underline{x} \\
&= \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \int f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \, \mathrm{d}\underline{x} \\
&= \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} 1 \\
&= 0.
\end{align*}

Here, we assumed the second *regularity condition*:

> **Regularity Condition 2:** We assumed we can interchange the integral and second derivative in the step
> $$
> \int \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}  f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \int f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) \,\mathrm{d}\underline{x}
> $$

Therefore, we can conclude Step 3 with the final result:

$$
\mathrm{Var}(U) = \mathcal{I}_n(\theta).
$$

---

**Step 4 (Proving $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\theta}, U) = 1$):**

By definition,

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\theta}, U) = \mathrm{E}\big[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)\,U\big].
$$

Using the same result used in steps 2 and 3:
$$
U(\theta;\underline{x}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \log f(\underline{x}\mid \theta) = \frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)},
$$

we have
$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta} U] 
= \int \hat{\theta}(\underline{x}) \,\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\underline{x}.
$$

Since $\hat{\theta}$ is *constant* in $\theta$ and assuming we can interchange the derivative and integral, we arrive at:

$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta} U] 
= \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \int \hat{\theta}(\underline{x}) f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)\,\mathrm{d}\underline{x}.
$$

This assumption forms our third regularity condition:

> **Regularity Condition 3:** We assumed we can interchange the integral and derivative in the step
> $$
>  \int \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\left(\hat{\theta}(\underline{x}) f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)\right)\,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \int \hat{\theta}(\underline{x}) f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)\,\mathrm{d}\underline{x}
> $$

Note now that $\int \hat{\theta}(\underline{x}) f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)\,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]$ and, since we assumed $\hat{\theta}$ is **unbiased**, we have
$$
\int \hat{\theta}(\underline{x}) f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)\,\mathrm{d}\underline{x} = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] = \theta.
$$
Hence,
$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta} U] = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\,\theta = 1.
$$

Also, from Step 2, $\mathrm{E}[U]=0$. Therefore,

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\theta}, U) = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta} U] - \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]\,\mathrm{E}[U] = 1 - \theta \cdot 0 = 1.
$$

---

**Conclusion:**

Putting Steps 1–4 together:

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \;\geq\; \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\theta},U)^2}{\mathrm{Var}(U)} \;=\; \frac{1^2}{\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)} \;=\; \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)}.
$$

This completes the proof of the **Cramér–Rao inequality**.

:::


::: {.callout-warning}
#### Non-Examinable Content
The *regularity conditions* required for the [CRLB]{title="Cramér–Rao Lower Bound"} are **not examinable**. 

Informally, these conditions rule out “badly behaved” cases; for example, densities $f(x\mid\theta)$ with infinite variance, infinite expectation, or parameter-dependent support. They also justify steps such as interchanging derivatives and integrals in the proof.

If you are curious, see the non-examinable proof in @prf-crlb.
:::


::: {#def-efficiency}
#### Efficiency of an Estimator

* An unbiased estimator is called **efficient** if its variance *achieves* the [CRLB]{title="Cramér–Rao Lower Bound"} exactly:

  $$
  \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)}.
  $$
* A sequence of estimators $\hat{\theta}_n$ is **asymptotically efficient** if, as the sample size grows, its variance approaches the [CRLB]{title="Cramér–Rao Lower Bound"}[^asymp-equiv]:
  $$
  \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_n)}{1/\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)} \;=\; 1,
  $$
  where $\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)$ is the <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher information @prp-fisher-one-obs]</span> for the **whole** sample of size $n$.

:::

::: {#cor-crlb-efficiency appearance="minimal"}

### Asymptotic Variance of an Efficient Estimator

By the CRLB and <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher Information for IID Data @prp-fisher-one-obs]</span>, the variance of an efficient estimator decreases at rate $1/n$ as the sample size increases.

:::

## The Asymptotic Distribution of the MLE

Previously, we introduced <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic @imp-term-asymptotic]</span> properties of estimators.

In particular, we saw that we can determine the asymptotic <span class="xref-no-num">[sampling distribution @def-sampling-distribution]</span> of an estimator:

>  The <span class="xref-no-num">[Central Limit Theorem @thm-clt]</span> told us that the sampling distribution of the <span class="xref-no-num">[sample mean @def-sample-mean]</span> is approximately Normal for large $n$.

This gave us a first example of the principle: with enough data, many estimators behave like a Normal random variable around the true parameter.

A much more general and powerful result is that maximum likelihood estimators also satisfy this property.

This is a regular-model result, not a guarantee for every likelihood. Boundary parameters, non-identifiable models, or strongly irregular likelihoods can produce non-Normal behaviour.

::: {#thm-asymp-mle}

### Asymptotic Distribution of the MLE

Let $\hat{\theta}_n$ denote the <span class="xref-no-num">[maximum likelihood estimator @def-mle]</span> based on $n$ i.i.d. samples $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ drawn from the same distribution with PDF/PMF $f(x \mid \theta)$.

Under *regularity conditions*, the MLE has the following asymptotic distribution:
$$
\sqrt{n}\,(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta) \;\xrightarrow{\,d\,}\; \mathcal{N} \big(0, \mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1}\big),
$$

where $\mathcal{I}_1(\theta) \;=\; -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \log f(X \mid \theta) \right]$ is the <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher Information @prp-fisher-one-obs]</span> for **a single observation**.

:::

::: {#prf-asymp-mle}
### Not Examinable

The full proof uses tools such as Taylor expansions of the score function and the Central Limit Theorem for sums of random variables.

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Non-Examinable Content
The *regularity conditions* required for the Asymptotic Distribution of the MLE are **not examinable**. 
:::

In this course, the main use of @thm-asymp-mle will be to approximate the MLE distribution using the Normal distribution for sufficiently large $n$:

::: {#def-asymp-mle-approx}
#### Approximate Sampling Distribution of the MLE

From the <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic distribution of the MLE @thm-asymp-mle]</span>, we obtain the following approximation:
$$
\hat{\theta}_n \;\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\; 
\mathcal N\!\left(\theta,\; \tfrac{1}{n}\,\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1}\right),
\qquad \text{for large } n.
$$
Equivalently, using the <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher Information @prp-fisher-one-obs]</span> for the whole sample $\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)$, and using $\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) = n\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)$, we have the approximation
$$
\hat{\theta}_n \;\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\; 
\mathcal N\!\left(\theta,\; \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)^{-1}\right),
\qquad \text{for large } n.
$$
The corresponding theoretical large-sample standard error is $\mathcal I_n(\theta)^{-1/2}$. Because $\theta$ is unknown, it must be estimated in applications. One common **plug-in expected-information** estimate is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_{\mathrm{exp}}
=\mathcal I_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}})^{-1/2}.
$$

This yields the practical variance estimate $\mathcal I_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}})^{-1}$. A second option uses the observed curvature defined below. These estimated standard errors underpin approximate confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.
:::

::: {#def-observed-fisher}
#### Observed Information

For fixed observed data $\underline x$, the **observed information** is the realised negative curvature of the log-likelihood:
$$
j_n(\theta;\underline x)
=-\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\ell(\theta;\underline x).
$$
Evaluating it at the observed MLE gives another estimated standard error,
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_{\mathrm{obs}}
=j_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}};\underline x)^{-1/2}.
$$

Do not confuse $j_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}};\underline x)$ with $\mathcal I_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}})$. The former uses the curvature of the realised log-likelihood; the latter evaluates an **expected** curvature at an estimated parameter. They are often close in large regular samples, but they need not be identical.
:::

::: {#exm-asymp-mle-pois}

### Asymptotic Distribution of the Poisson MLE

Suppose $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ is an i.i.d. random sample from a $\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ distribution.  

We know that the maximum likelihood estimator for $\lambda$ is  

$$
\hat{\lambda} = \bar{X}.
$$

What is the asymptotic distribution of $\hat{\lambda} = \bar{X}$ as $n \to \infty$?

```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Solution</strong></summary>
```

In @exm-poisson-fisher, we saw the Fisher information for one Poisson observation is  

$$
\mathcal{I}_1(\lambda) = \frac{1}{\lambda}.
$$

For $n$ independent observations this scales to  

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\lambda) = \frac{n}{\lambda}.
$$

Therefore,
$$
\frac{1}{\mathcal{I}_n(\lambda)} = \frac{\lambda}{n}.
$$

It follows immediately from @thm-asymp-mle that

$$
\hat{\lambda} \;\;\stackrel{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\;\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\lambda,\; \tfrac{\lambda}{n}\right),
\quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
$$


```{=html}
</details>
```

:::

For the Bernoulli model, explain why $\bar Y$ is simultaneously an unbiased estimator and the MLE, while still being a random quantity before the data are observed.
:::

## Chapter summary

- Starting from a model, the main route is
  $$
  \text{joint model}\longrightarrow L(\theta;\underline x)
  \longrightarrow \ell(\theta;\underline x)
  \longrightarrow \hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}
  \longrightarrow \text{information and an estimated standard error}.
  $$
- A likelihood treats the observed data as fixed and compares parameter values; it is not a probability distribution over the parameter.
- Solving the score equation only finds candidates: the parameter space, boundaries, curvature, and global maximum must still be checked.
- Expected Fisher information and observed information describe related but distinct curvatures; large-sample standard errors and Normal approximations depend on regularity conditions.


[^geometric-mean]: **Geometric mean.** One can write $\prod_{i=1}^n x_i = \bar{x}_g^n$ where $\bar{x}_g = \left(\prod_{i=1}^n x_i \right)^{1/n}$ is the *geometric mean*. This reformulation is rarely useful in practice, so it’s usually best to leave the product as it is.

[^asymp-equiv]: **Asymptotic Equivalence.** Equivalently, we could say $\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_n) \sim \tfrac{1}{\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)}$, where "$\sim$" here means *asymptotically equivalent*.
